title: An abelian-variety isogeny admits an integer quasi-inverse
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $A,B$ be abelian varieties over $k$ [def-sc-abelian-variety], and let $u:A\to B$ be an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny]. There exist an integer $n\geq1$ and a $k$-group-scheme homomorphism $v:B\to A$ [def-sc-group-scheme] such that
$$v\circ u=[n]_A,\qquad u\circ v=[n]_B,$$
where $[n]$ denotes multiplication by $n$ [def-sc-mult-n]. No perfection of $k$, separability of $u$, or restriction on the characteristic is assumed.

source.place: I Remark 8.6, printed p.36, and I Proposition 8.10, printed pp.38–39: factor multiplication through the quotient by the kernel. A positive integer annihilating the finite commutative kernel is supplied by Milne Algebraic Groups, Proposition 11.32, printed p.221.

proof.text: Put $K=\ker u$ and let $i:K\to A$ be its inclusion. By [def-sc-isogeny] and [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup], $K$ is a finite group scheme and $K(R)=\ker(u(R))$. By [lem-sc-av-commutative], $A$ is commutative, hence so is its subgroup $K$. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-group-scheme-order-annihilator]: for $n=\dim_k\Gamma(K,\mathcal O_K)$ one has $n\geq1$ and $[n]_K=0$. Consequently $[n]_A\circ i=0$, because a homomorphism commutes with repeated addition [def-sc-mult-n].

source.place: Proposition 11.32, printed p.221; AV I Remark 8.6, printed p.36

proof.text: By [lem-sc-isogeny-degree], $u$ is finite and flat, and by [def-sc-isogeny] it is surjective. A finite morphism is affine [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], so for every affine open $V\subseteq B$, $u^{-1}(V)$ is affine and maps onto $V$. Taking this single affine open in the definition [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering] shows that $\{u:A\to B\}$ is an fpqc covering.

source.place: Tag 022B, definition-fpqc-covering; Milne AV I Remark 8.6 quotient input

proof.text: The group operations give inverse morphisms $A\times_kK\to A\times_BA$, $(a,t)\mapsto(a,a+i(t))$, and $(a,a\prime)\mapsto(a,a\prime-a)$; the second component of the latter factors through $K$ since $u(a\prime-a)=0$ [lem-sc-kernel-subgroup]. The composites are identities by the group laws [def-sc-group-scheme]. Under this identification the projections are $a$ and $a+i(t)$. Their composites with $[n]_A$ agree, since $[n]_A(a+i(t))=[n]_A(a)+i([n]_K(t))=[n]_A(a)$ by Step 1 and [def-sc-mult-n]. These are identities of morphisms formed from group operations, including on nonreduced test schemes.

source.place: I Remark 8.6, printed p.36, kernel quotient calculation

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] to the singleton covering $u$ of Step 2, target scheme $A$, and morphism $[n]_A:A\to A$. Step 3 is exactly its compatibility condition on the self-overlap. It gives a unique scheme morphism $v:B\to A$ with $v\circ u=[n]_A$. This morphism is over $k$: the structure morphisms $B\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $B\xrightarrow{v}A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ agree after $u$, and uniqueness in the same descent statement, now with target $\operatorname{Spec}k$, makes them equal.

Let $m_A,m_B$ be the group laws. The maps $v\circ m_B$ and $m_A\circ(v\times v)$ from $B\times_kB$ to $A$ agree after $u\times u$, because $u$ is a homomorphism and $v u=[n]_A$, which is a homomorphism [def-sc-mult-n, lem-sc-av-commutative]. More explicitly both restrictions send $(a,a\prime)$ to $[n]_A(a)+[n]_A(a\prime)$. The maps $\operatorname{id}_A\times u:A\times_kA\to A\times_kB$ and $u\times\operatorname{id}_B:A\times_kB\to B\times_kB$ are separately base changes of $u$, hence fpqc coverings by [lem-galois-fpqc-covering-base-change]. Apply uniqueness in [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] first to the former and then to the latter to obtain $v m_B=m_A(v\times v)$. Also $v(e_B)=v u(e_A)=[n]_A(e_A)=e_A$; thus $v$ is a group-scheme homomorphism [def-sc-group-scheme].

Finally $(u v)u=u[n]_A=[n]_Bu$, the second equality being the repeated-addition identity for the homomorphism $u$ [def-sc-mult-n]. The uniqueness clause of [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] for the covering $u$ and target $B$ gives $u v=[n]_B$. Together with Step 4 and the positive integer $n$ of Step 1 this proves both required identities. No step assumed perfection, separability, or that $n$ is invertible in $k$.

source.place: I Remark 8.6, printed p.36; Stacks Tag 023Q for cancellation
